Contact of Ferry Ray Stoker, Jr. with Floating
Dock
On September 10, 2024, about 1823 local time, the vehicle and passenger
ferry Ray Stoker, Jr. experienced a loss of propulsion control while underway in
Galveston Channel, struck a floating dock at US Coast Guard Base Galveston, in
Galveston, Texas, and grounded in about 4 feet of water (see figure 1 and figure 2).1
Six crewmembers, seven passengers, and three vehicles were on board the ferry.
There were no injuries, and no pollution was reported. Damage to the vessel and
dock was estimated at $373,800.2

1 Factual Information
1.1 Background
The 263-foot-long, welded-steel, open-deck vehicle and passenger ferry, Ray
Stoker, Jr., owned and operated by the Texas Department of Transportation, was built
at Moss Point Marine shipyard in Mississippi in 1996. The ferry provided free, 24-hour
vehicle and passenger service between Bolivar Peninsula, Texas, and Galveston
Island, Texas, and had a maximum capacity of 70 vehicles.
The Ray Stoker, Jr. was a double-ended ferry with identical wheelhouses and
propulsion units at each end (see figure 3). This configuration allowed the vessel to
approach and leave its slips without turning around. Typically, the ferry’s “A end”
docked in Bolivar; the “B end” docked in Galveston. Watchstanding deck
crewmembers repositioned themselves from one end to the other between transits.
Each round trip began at the Galveston terminal, where the ferry was docked when
not in use.
Figure 3. Profile view of Ray Stoker, Jr., showing starboard side view of vessel with A end
(Bolivar) and B end (Galveston) labeled. (Background source: Texas Department of
Transportation)
Two cycloidal propellers, one at each end of the vessel, provided propulsion
(thrust and steering control).3 Each propeller was mechanically driven by a
12-cylinder marine diesel engine. The propulsion control system was upgraded
3 A cycloidal propeller consists of a large, rotating, horizontally configured circular disk
beneath the vessel, driven by the main propulsion engine. The disk is fitted with a series of controllable
pitch blades protruding vertically downward from the disk. The magnitude and direction of thrust are
determined by the rotational speed of the disk, and the direction of thrust is determined by the
positioning of the blade angles.

in 2020 from a mechanical to an electronic system. There were control stations in
each of the wheelhouses and in the engine operating station (EOS), as well as a local
emergency control station at each propulsion unit. During typical operations, the
propulsion system was controlled from one of the wheelhouses. The wheelhouse
control system consisted of two joysticks mounted on the operating console: one
positioned by the operator’s left hand, and one by the operator’s right hand on either
side of a sliding chair (see figure 4). The joysticks could be operated in synchronized
or manual mode. When in synchronized mode, the right joystick controlled both the
forward and aft propulsion units, and the left joystick controlled the side to side
(athwart) movement of the forward unit. In manual mode, the left joystick controlled
the forward propulsion unit, and the right joystick controlled the aft unit.
Figure 4. “B end” wheelhouse of Ray Stoker, Jr. (“A end” similar).
An angled touch panel was located forward of each joystick on the console,
between the joysticks and the wheelhouse windows. The two touch panels (in each
wheelhouse and in the EOS) provided system status, operational information, and
system alarms. The ferry operator could make operational changes to the vessel’s
propulsion system on the touch panels, activating icons to change views, change
operating parameters, adjust engine speed (idle, medium, high), or switch operating

1.2 Event Sequence
On September 10, at 1100, a crew of six, consisting of a captain (who had over
25 years in the maritime industry and about 5 months with the ferries), three
deckhands, a chief engineer, and an oiler, reported to the vessel. The captain and
deckhand went to the wheelhouse, and the chief engineer and oiler stood watch in
the engine room.
At 1144, the Ray Stoker, Jr. departed Galveston for the first 2.7-mile round trip
of the day between Galveston and Bolivar. Throughout the rest of the day, the crew
completed 13 trips across Galveston Bay, averaging about 18 minutes for each round
trip, transiting at 10 knots. The largest complement of the day was the second trip
from Bolivar with one truck, 46 cars, and 144 passengers.
At 1810, the Ray Stoker, Jr. departed Bolivar for the fourteenth and final trip of
the day, bound for Galveston with seven passengers and three cars aboard. The
captain controlled the ferry from the “B end” wheelhouse, while the deckhand
completed paperwork. The propulsion system was being operated in synchronized
mode. The joysticks were used to input commands to control the pitch of the
propulsion system, providing longitudinal and transverse thrust for propulsion and
steering. The captain stated that, at this time, skies were overcast, with winds about
10-15 knots from the northeast, and there was no appreciable current.
As the ferry approached its dock, at 10 knots in the Galveston Channel, with
Coast Guard Base Galveston about 300 feet off its port side, the captain adjusted
both joysticks for the propulsion system to their neutral positions to slow the vessel to
about 8 knots and to maintain its current heading. Once the vessel’s speed was
reduced to 8 knots, the captain adjusted the joysticks to re-apply power and maintain
8 knots at the same heading. However, the vessel began turning to port toward the
Coast Guard base. The captain tried to correct the steering using both joysticks, but
there was no response from either joystick. According to the captain, there were no
alarms or abnormalities with the control system. The vessel slowed in speed but
continued turning to port toward the Coast Guard docks.

The captain called the chief engineer in the EOS and advised him of the loss of
control. At the chief engineer’s instruction, the captain clicked the command icon to
verify his station was in control and in synchronized mode, but there was no change
in system status.
The chief engineer told investigators that he had experienced a similar loss of
propulsion control on another vessel equipped with the same propulsion control
system. He had rectified the situation by taking command control in the EOS and
sending control back to the captain in the wheelhouse. He referred to this process as
a “system reset.” (He stated that the previous loss of control was caused by an
overheated controller; the condition had been repaired on the Ray Stoker, Jr. and all
similar ferries by installing air conditioning units in the controllers.)
Using the touch panel icons in the EOS, the chief engineer transferred control
of the propulsion system down to the EOS, lowered the engines to idle speed, and
transferred the control back to the wheelhouse (after determining the system was
working properly from the EOS). The chief engineer told investigators that there had
been no alarms or any indications of issues with the system. While the chief engineer
was transferring the propulsion system, the captain used the public address system to
warn passengers to brace for impact, and deck crewmembers notified passengers to
brace themselves.
The deckhand left the wheelhouse and went down to the anchor and prepared
to release it when directed. The ferry continued turning to port until it had turned
about 90° and was parallel to a floating dock at the Coast Guard base. After the chief
engineer transferred control of the propulsion system back to the wheelhouse, the
captain regained control of the propulsion system, but about 1823, the Ray Stoker, Jr.
contacted a floating dock on the west end of the Coast Guard base at 1 knot (see
figure 5).

The ferry’s portside rub rail pushed the first piling supporting the floating dock
to the east, causing the piling to strike a metal railing and support structure of the
adjacent fixed boat lift dock. The last piling for the floating dock was also pushed to
the east and broke up the dock surrounding the piling (which was composed of
concrete and foam). The ferry’s lifeboat brackets rode up onto the floating dock,
damaging the concrete and the metal structures holding it in place. The ferry then
grounded in about 4 feet of water near the shoreline alongside the floating dock and
came to a stop. The dock was not in use by any Coast Guard vessels or personnel at
the time of the accident.
Immediately after the contact, crewmembers checked the Ray Stoker, Jr. for
water ingress and determined there was none. The captain and chief engineer tested

notified the Coast Guard and dispatch office and received permission to resume the

The vessel tied up at 1900. There were no injuries reported by crewmembers

1.3 Additional Information
1.3.1 Damage
After the casualty, divers surveyed the affected floating pier and noted broken
concrete under the floating pier and damaged rollers attached to the pilings. (The
floating pier had previously been damaged and was listing about 30–40° before
being struck by the Ray Stoker, Jr.) The pier had an estimated replacement value of
$368,800. Weeks after the accident, a storm further damaged the floating pier, which
led to its decommissioning and removal.
Damage to the Ray Stoker, Jr. consisted of scraped paint about 1 foot above
the waterline along the port side of the hull. Additionally, the portside rub rail had
about 3 feet of white paint transferred to it from the floating dock pilings. Steel
brackets under the lifeboat launching area were scraped, dented, and broken.
Damage was estimated at $5,000. The brackets were repaired or replaced by the
ferry’s shoreside maintenance team.
1.3.2 Postcasualty Troubleshooting
On September 13, service technicians from the cycloidal propulsion system
manufacturer reported to the Ray Stoker, Jr. to troubleshoot the loss of propulsion
control that occurred on September 10. Technicians created an offline device for the
system, checked the error file, and verified that no alarms were present during the
time of control loss. According to the technician’s report, it was unlikely that control
was lost from both ends at the same time by a condition that did not cause alarms,
and “only a complete loss of power or an extreme multi-point failure would cause
such a loss without alarms if the system was faulty.” Technicians and crew conducted
sea trials for 3 days to attempt to replicate the loss of control. During the trials, the
system operated as intended and no errors were observed.
The technicians concluded that the “station freeze” icon on one of the touch
panels had likely been activated, which would have caused joystick control to be
unresponsive without generating any alarms. Touching the station freeze icon would

propulsion units if the joysticks were adjusted. The captain said he had never used
the station freeze icon but understood it could be used to hold the vessel at a dock
with a constant propulsion setting.
Technicians discovered that when the plastic clip on a window shade chain
touched the station freeze icon on the touch panel, the station freeze function
activated (see figure 6). The captain could not confidently recall the position of the
window shade chains, nor whether he had adjusted any of the window shades during
the transit (which would have required moving the chain for each shade). According
to one deckhand, crewmembers would typically lower the shades when the sun was
“too bright” and raise the shades if the sun was going down. The captain stated that,
at times during previous transits, he had seen a window shade chain lying across the
control touch panel, and he usually removed it from the controls.

Technicians instructed crewmembers that, when cleaning the touch panels,
they should select a screen that would not have the ability to make operational
changes. The captain stated that he did not clean any touch panels on the evening of
the casualty.
1.3.3 Postcasualty Actions
As a result of the casualty and the postcasualty troubleshooting, Ray Stoker, Jr.
crewmembers mounted clips on the bulkheads to hold the window shade chains in

posted in each wheelhouse stating, “Please ensure blind lanyard does not come in
contact with [touch panel] screen.” The vessel’s management team instructed
crewmembers on three other ferries with similar touch panels to install fittings to
secure the plastic clips for the window shades so that they would not come into
contact with the station freeze icon on the control touch panels.
Management also updated their Vessel Safety Equipment Checklist to include
checking the chains were secured in the clips, and sent a memorandum on
September 23, 2024, to all captains and helmsmen, warning them of that the
wheelhouse station freeze icon could be inadvertently activated and instructing them
to ensure no items were placed over the touch panels. The memorandum also
directed crewmembers to check the station freeze function icon in the event control
was lost.
In July 2025, transparent plexiglass covers were installed on the
Robert H. Dedman, which had similar control arrangement. In August 2025,
transparent plexiglass covers were installed on the Ray Stoker, Jr (see figure 7). As of
the date of this report, installation was still pending on the remaining two ferries with

2 Analysis
While the vehicle and passenger ferry Ray Stoker, Jr. was underway from
Bolivar to Galveston, the crew experienced a loss of cycloidal propulsion system
control (thrust and steering control), and the ferry struck a floating pier at Coast
Guard Base Galveston before grounding and coming to a stop.
During the loss of cycloidal propulsion system control, the captain adjusted
both joysticks, but neither produced any speed or directional changes to either
propulsion unit. Postcasualty inspection of the system by the manufacturer’s service
technicians indicated that no alarms activated during the incident. Three days of sea
trials were conducted in an attempt to replicate the loss of control, but the system
operated as intended. Therefore, the vessel’s loss of cycloidal propulsion system
control was not caused by an issue with the propulsion control system.
The control touch panel for the cycloidal propulsion system had a “station
freeze” function that, when activated, would lock (or freeze) the joysticks in the last set
position. Technicians considered the possibility that an object could have
inadvertently activated this function. They tested the plastic clip on a window shade
chain by touching the clip to the touch panel, and the clip activated functions in the
same manner as an operator’s finger. Crewmembers in the wheelhouse did not recall
clicking the station freeze icon, and they stated that they had not cleaned the touch
panels during the transit. The captain stated that, at times during previous transits, he
had seen the wheelhouse window shade chain lying across a control touch panel, and
he usually removed it from the panel. Based on the time of the casualty (1823—about
an hour from sunset) and the number of crossings between Bolivar and Galveston,
the shade chain could have been adjusted at some point due to the ferry’s position
relative to the sun. According to one deckhand, they typically adjusted the shade if
the sun was “too bright” or going down. Adjusting the shade increased the potential
that the chain and its plastic clip, once released after adjustment by the operator,
would lay atop the touch panel. However, crewmembers in the wheelhouse did not
recall adjusting the window shade during the transit. If the shade chain and its plastic
clip had been left lying across the touch panel, the clip could have activated the
station freeze function during the transit, unbeknownst to the operator. Following the
accident, the operating company installed transparent plexiglass covers over the
control touch panels on the Ray Stoker, Jr. and instructed ferry crewmembers to
install fittings to secure window shade chains so that they would not come into
contact with the panels.

3 Conclusions
3.1 Probable Cause
The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause
of the contact of the ferry Ray Stoker, Jr. with a floating dock was likely a wheelhouse
window shade chain clip activating the station freeze function on a propulsion control
touch panel, resulting in a temporary loss of propulsion control.
